title: Here Are the Service Gaps Close to Home!
subtitle: Elderly Centre Accessibility and Community Site Selection in Hong Kong

sections.title: Introduction
sections.intro: Where do areas with a high share of older residents also have residential land far from Neighbourhood Elderly Centres (NECs)?

slides.title: Older resident numbers and population shares
slides.summary: The map shows the number of residents aged 65 or above; the screening uses their share of each area’s total population.
slides.text: A large older population and a high older-resident share describe different aspects of a community. We use the share for screening and retain headcounts and total population to interpret the results. Map symbols summarise entire statistical areas; they do not locate individual residents.

before.text: The screening identifies priority areas for community service review.

before.description: Priority areas for community service review. Screened from 210 assessed STPUGs using two P60 conditions and an 800 m NEC radius.

sections.title: Data and Objectives
sections.intro: We combine census statistics, residential land and elderly-centre locations to identify areas for review, then compare how model locations and existing venues could extend residential accessibility coverage.

slides.title: Elderly centre locations
slides.summary: The baseline contains 215 distinct NEC locations. An alternative scenario also includes 62 District Elderly Community Centre (DECC) locations.
slides.text: The Social Welfare Department (SWD) records were retrieved on 2 November 2026. The 216 NEC premises records occupy 215 distinct coordinates, so coincident records are merged for distance calculations.

slides.title: Population and residential denominators
slides.summary: The older-resident share is the number of residents aged 65 or above divided by the total population of the same small tertiary planning unit group (STPUG).
slides.text: The analysis uses 211 STPUGs from the 2021 Census geography. Residential proximity can be assessed for 210 groups. Group 295 has no assigned residential cells and is excluded from the joint screen. Interpret a high older-resident share alongside the older-resident count, total population and residential area.

sections.title: Methodology
sections.intro: We apply separate cutoffs to population age structure and residential accessibility, then examine how the shortlist changes under alternative assumptions.

before.caption: Census statistics, residential cells and facility locations are combined to calculate two indicators, apply the joint screening rule, test alternative assumptions and compare local reference locations.

before.text: This study uses the 60th percentile (P60) as its screening standard for two indicators across the 210 assessed STPUGs: the share of residents aged 65 or above and the share of residential land more than 800 m from the nearest NEC. Every group has equal weight. The thresholds are approximately 20% and 31%, respectively. Groups meeting or exceeding both P60 thresholds enter the shortlist. Each condition is met by 84 groups, and 13 meet both.

Distances are calculated in Hong Kong 1980 Grid (EPSG:2326). Each 10 m residential-cell centre is assigned to an STPUG, and its straight-line distance to the nearest NEC anywhere in Hong Kong is calculated, including centres outside that group. This study sets 800 m as its baseline coverage standard. Cells at or within 800 m count as covered. The outside-area share equals the number of residential cells beyond 800 m divided by all assigned residential cells in that group. Each cell represents 100 m² of residential ground area.

The 27 scenarios combine three age-share percentiles (P50, P60 and P70), three outside-area percentiles and three radii (500, 800 and 1,000 m). The outside-area distribution is recalculated for each radius. A separate test holds the two baseline numerical cutoffs fixed and changes only the radius. Age-cohort tests use cohort-specific P60 age-share cutoffs. The NEC plus DECC scenario tests a broader facility network.

Within each shortlisted group, one residential cell nearest the centre of each occupied 200 m grid square is used as a candidate location. A provides the greatest additional residential-area coverage among these candidates. B provides the greatest stand-alone gain among candidates at least 400 m from A. C maximises the remaining gain after A has been added. Model locations are compared with registered community venues and DECC premises.

Geographical proximity is one dimension of accessibility (Geurs & van Wee, 2004). This study uses residential coverage to compare access to elderly centres and identify priority areas for service review.

sections.title: Spatial Analysis
sections.intro: We first examine the distributions of age share and residential accessibility, then identify the joint shortlist and compare possible additions in three local cases.

slides.title: Residential outside-area shares cluster at zero and 100 percent
slides.summary: At 800 m, 80 of the 210 assessed groups have no residential land beyond the NEC radius, while 42 have all residential land beyond it. The remaining 88 groups lie between these extremes.
slides.text: The concentration of values at 0% and 100% affects percentile cutoffs and map classes. Area-wide shading identifies the statistical group. Residential land serves as a spatial proxy for potential service demand, and the outside-area share highlights where this demand is distant from existing NECs.

slides.title: Thirteen areas meet both criteria
slides.summary: The main screen requires both the older-resident share and the residential outside-area share to meet their respective P60 cutoffs.
slides.text: The 13 shortlisted groups are 131, 140, 155, 162, 175S, 525, 545, 620S, 758, 821, 825, 920 and 944. For comparison, the fixed 20% age-share and 30% outside-area rule selects 14 groups, including group 149. Group 295 remains unassessed because it has no assigned residential cells.

slides.title: Explore assumptions
slides.summary: Use the explorer to compare the P60 rule with fixed cutoffs, alternative age cohorts and the NEC plus DECC network.
slides.text: The explorer displays population and residential-area denominators for each group. A larger outside-area share indicates a larger accessibility gap under the selected settings. Selection frequencies show how consistently groups enter the shortlist across scenarios.

slides.title: Sensitivity remains visible
slides.summary: The scenario maps show how often individual groups are selected; the 27-cell comparison chart shows how many groups are selected under each combination of assumptions.
slides.text: Use the distance and age matrices to inspect the baseline shortlist under alternative settings. In the 27-scenario chart, rows indicate age-share percentiles and columns indicate outside-area percentiles. Compare changes in membership as well as changes in the number selected. Similar totals do not guarantee similar shortlists.

slides.title: Wan Chai group 131
slides.summary: Most residential land in this group lies beyond the NEC radius, although the total residential area is only 12.00 ha.
slides.text: Group 131 has 5,290 residents aged 65 or above (20.20%) and 12.00 ha of residential land. Of that land, 11.69 ha lies beyond the existing NEC 800 m radius. Model A and the community-venue alternative each bring all 11.69 ha within the modelled radius. Nearby DECC locations provide an additional comparison for local service planning.

infographics.title: 11.69 ha
infographics.description: Newly covered residential land with either model A or the community venue. Wan Chai 131.

slides.title: Ta Kwu Ling group 620S
slides.summary: Assess a second location by the residential area it adds after the first location is in place.
slides.text: All 110.36 ha of residential land in group 620S lies beyond the existing NEC 800 m radius. Model A adds 31.01 ha. B covers 28.63 ha on its own but adds only 3.05 ha after A. Choosing C for the remaining gap adds 25.09 ha after A, giving 56.10 ha in total. In a separate arrangement, Ta Kwu Ling Community Hall adds 19.62 ha on its own. These results compare the A-plus-C arrangement with the stand-alone community-hall option.

infographics.title: 56.10 ha
infographics.description: Total additional residential coverage with A + C: 31.01 ha from A, then 25.09 ha from C. Ta Kwu Ling 620S.

slides.title: Cheung Chau group 920
slides.summary: Cheung Chau Community Hall provides a documented venue to compare with the model reference location.
slides.text: Group 920 has 4,450 residents aged 65 or above (22.51%) and 56.54 ha of residential land. Model A adds 28.93 ha of coverage, compared with 26.71 ha for Cheung Chau Community Hall, approximately 92.3% of A’s gain. B adds no further area after A. In the separate hall-first arrangement, H2 denotes a complementary second model location that adds 4.01 ha after the hall.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.intro: The joint screen identifies 13 statistical groups as priorities for local service planning.

before.text: The analysis identifies where a relatively high older-resident share coincides with residential land distant from NEC premises. This provides a reproducible starting point for local service planning using the P60 screening rule and the 800 m coverage standard.

Existing venues provide concrete options for community service provision, while model locations indicate where additional residential-area coverage could be concentrated. Second locations are compared by their marginal gain after the first location is added. A Hong Kong-wide plan can build on these local comparisons by incorporating resource constraints and accounting for overlapping coverage across areas.

The analysis combines 2021 population and land-use data with facility records from 2026. It measures accessibility through residential ground area and straight-line distance. Future work can incorporate building-level population, walking routes and service capacity to refine local planning.
